![](images/svg/margin_renewal_jitter_lease_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two gray horizontal bars labeled renewal due at 50 and latest at 55, both ending left of a dashed red vertical line labeled lease 60 milliseconds, with a light red wash beyond it."}
*A renewal may run `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_jitter_str` late; at `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_lapse_str` late the lease lapses.*
:::

A chunk whose inference waits behind the same traffic renews the lease late, and there the lease rule of @sec-nervous-coupled-budget leaves `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_jitter_str` of renewal jitter above the `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_period_str` chunk period. Host contention may therefore stretch the chunk policy's `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_infer_str` inference by at most `{python} HostContentionAllowance.stretch_pct_str` percent, and by less in practice, because the same allowance also holds the proposer's own jitter and the jitter of the board-level link to the microcontroller (@sec-placement-isolation-decisions). A renewal `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_lapse_str` late lets the lease lapse and stops the machine. With the stated isolation, age checks, and feasible fallback intact, excess contention costs availability: the permission path refuses delay outside the qualified budget. That conclusion depends on those premises, including continued access to valid local evidence.

How long a burst holds the bus also matters to the camera interface itself. Ingest engines utilize direct memory access ring buffers with double or triple buffering to decouple arrival interrupts from consumer reading threads. If host memory bus contention delays DMA completion beyond what the CSI-2 receiver hardware FIFO can buffer, the receiver suffers an overrun and silently drops the frame. A dropped frame doubles the effective observation interval between samples, and downstream state observers must treat the missing update as an age or sequence fault rather than assuming that fresh scene geometry will arrive on schedule.

The hardware mechanisms governing frame delivery (DMA rings, IOMMU mappings, and DRAM arbitration) are treated by @hennessy2019computer and @bryant2015computer. For this chapter's decision, the quantity that matters is capture-to-consumer age and its tail under the intended camera workload.

An on-time frame answers only when the scene was sampled. Where the objects in it are, and how far that estimate can be trusted, is a separate question, and the error in that answer is spent from the same clearance.

## Spatial Error and Clearance Bounds {#sec-perception-error-clearance}

When perception places a rack upright a few centimeters farther from the base's path than it actually stands, the base plans its pass with those centimeters missing from the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.side_clearance_str` side clearance it keeps from the racks, and no stage of the pipeline decided to spend them. Once downstream control logic uses an estimated coordinate to authorize motion, a spatial error becomes a physical displacement, spent out of the same clearance that keeps the machine off the obstacle. Transforming a sensor observation into a clearance claim requires **metric grounding**\index{Metric grounding!definition}, which maps raw detector measurements into geometric space. This grounding relies on unprojecting two-dimensional sensor coordinates into three dimensions, an inversion that assumes known optics, rigid mounting, and predictable surface properties.

The mathematical principles of projection and triangulation [@hartley2003multiple; @szeliski2022computer] govern how measurement noise converts into spatial displacement. In two-view streaming perception, two cameras with optical centers $\mathbf{o}_1, \mathbf{o}_2$ observe a physical 3D scene point $\mathbf{p}$. The baseline vector $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ connecting $\mathbf{o}_1$ and $\mathbf{o}_2$, along with the point $\mathbf{p}$, forms the **epipolar plane**\index{Epipolar geometry!epipolar plane}. The intersection of the baseline with each image plane defines the **epipoles** $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2$.

For image coordinates $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2$ expressed in homogeneous pixel coordinates, the rigid spatial transformation $(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}) \in \text{SE}(3)$ relating the camera frames establishes the fundamental **epipolar constraint**\index{Epipolar constraint!definition}:
$$\mathbf{x}_2^\top \mathbf{F}_{\text{fund}} \, \mathbf{x}_1 = 0$$
where $\mathbf{F}_{\text{fund}} = \mathbf{K}_2^{-\top} \mathbf{E} \, \mathbf{K}_1^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is the **Fundamental matrix**\index{Fundamental matrix}, and $\mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{t}]_\times \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is the **Essential matrix**\index{Essential matrix} (with $[\mathbf{t}]_\times$ denoting the skew-symmetric matrix of the baseline translation). The vector $\mathbf{l}_2 = \mathbf{F}_{\text{fund}} \mathbf{x}_1$ defines the **epipolar line** in the second image; any physical correspondence $\mathbf{x}_2$ must lie strictly along $\mathbf{l}_2$.

In a calibrated **rectified stereo rig**\index{Stereo rectification!epipolar lines}, both images are digitally warped onto a common virtual image plane parallel to the baseline ($\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{t} = [b, 0, 0]^\top$). Rectification forces epipolar lines to be exactly parallel and collinear with horizontal scanlines ($y_1 = y_2$). This geometric transformation reduces an expensive two-dimensional correspondence search, the kind optical-flow networks perform, to a one-dimensional search along the same horizontal scanline, which neural stereo networks such as RAFT-Stereo evaluate as a correlation volume [@lipson2021raftstereo]: disparity is simply $d = u_1 - u_2$, recovering metric depth $z = \frac{f b}{d}$.

When mechanical vibration, chassis twist, or thermal expansion induces uncalibrated relative pitch or roll between cameras, or when rolling-shutter readout shears scanlines during robot rotation, the true physical correspondence shifts vertically off the horizontal epipolar line ($\Delta y \neq 0$). The 1D correlation cost volume fails or locks onto spurious texture matches across adjacent rows, producing severe triangulation outliers. Differentiating the unprojection $z = \frac{f b}{d}$ with respect to disparity gives a negative signed derivative; its magnitude yields the small-error relation (@eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty):
$$|\delta z| \approx \frac{z^2}{f b} |\delta d|$$ {#eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty}
where $\delta d$ is a small disparity error. If $\delta d$ denotes a disparity standard deviation $\sigma_d$, first-order propagation gives $\sigma_z\approx z^2\sigma_d/(fb)$. Doubling range quadruples this modeled standard deviation at fixed $f$, $b$, and $\sigma_d$. For distant landmarks, an estimator instead carries depth as inverse depth[^fn-inverse-depth-parametrization] $\rho = 1/z = d / (f b)$. Differentiating with respect to disparity yields:
$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial d} = \frac{1}{f b} = \text{constant}$$
Because this derivative is independent of distance, measurement errors in disparity map linearly into inverse depth ($\delta \rho = \frac{1}{f b} \delta d$). This linear mapping provides **inverse-depth metric grounding**\index{Inverse-depth metric grounding!definition}, which can improve numerical conditioning for distant landmarks when the disparity-error model is appropriate. It does not eliminate mismatch outliers or guarantee estimator stability. A pulsed time-of-flight sensor instead estimates $z=c\Delta t/2$; its range error depends on its timing and detection mechanism and may be approximately flat over a specified operating region.

[^fn-inverse-depth-parametrization]: **Inverse-Depth Parametrization**\index{Mathematics!inverse-depth}: @civera2008inverse introduced it for monocular SLAM, where a newly seen landmark may lie arbitrarily far away. Storing $\rho = 1/z$ lets a point at infinity enter the estimate as $\rho = 0$ with finite variance, where a depth coordinate would need an infinite one, so near and distant landmarks share one well-conditioned representation. The derivation is in @sec-appendix-ml-spatial.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-stereo-depth-error
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STEREO DEPTH-ERROR SCALE AND BASELINE THERMAL BIAS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The stereo worked example of @sec-perception-error-clearance and
# │          the thermal-expansion footnote of @sec-perception-observation-contract.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how the one-sigma stereo depth scale grows with squared range,
# │          why adding it to a clearance kept along the viewing ray does not
# │          give an inset, and
# │          what an unmodeled baseline change does to depth at long range.
# │ Show:    sigma_z 12.5 mm at 2 m and 312.5 mm at 10 m; a 150 mm ray clearance plus
# │          one sigma 162.5 mm and 462.5 mm; 10 mm depth bias at 20 m.
# │ How:     sigma_z = z^2 sigma_d / (f b); |dz| = z |db| / b.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_display_math, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class StereoDepthError:
    """One-sigma stereo depth scale on an illustrative rig, and baseline thermal bias."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    b = 0.20 * meter  # category: illustrative (stereo baseline)
    f_px = 800.0  # category: illustrative (focal length, pixels)
    sigma_d_px = 0.5  # category: illustrative (disparity standard deviation, pixels)
    z_near = 2.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    z_far = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    db = 0.1 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (unmodeled baseline change)
    z_thermal = 20.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    c_ray = 150.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (clearance kept along the viewing ray)
    z_rack = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (localization allowance)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    sigma_z_near = (z_near**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    sigma_z_far = (z_far**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    naive_near = (c_ray + sigma_z_near).to(ureg.millimeter)
    naive_far = (c_ray + sigma_z_far).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dz_thermal = (z_thermal * db / b).to(ureg.millimeter)
    sigma_z_rack = (z_rack**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    z_star_loc = ((delta_loc * f_px * b / sigma_d_px) ** 0.5).to(meter)  # range where sigma_z = delta_loc
    z_star_side = ((side_clearance * f_px * b / sigma_d_px) ** 0.5).to(meter)  # range where sigma_z = side clearance
    z_star_side_half_b = ((side_clearance * f_px * (b / 2) / sigma_d_px) ** 0.5).to(meter)  # checkpoint: halved baseline

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(sigma_z_near.magnitude - 12.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected near sigma_z: {sigma_z_near}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_far.magnitude - 312.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected far sigma_z: {sigma_z_far}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_far / sigma_z_near - 25.0) < 1e-9, "Depth scale must grow with squared range")
    check(abs(dz_thermal.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected thermal depth bias: {dz_thermal}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_rack.magnitude - 3.78) < 0.01, f"Unexpected sigma_z at the rack end: {sigma_z_rack}")
    check(abs(z_star_loc.magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected delta_loc crossover range: {z_star_loc}")
    check(abs(z_star_side.magnitude - 6.93) < 0.005, f"Unexpected side-clearance crossover range: {z_star_side}")
    check(z_rack < z_star_loc < z_star_side < z_far, "Notebook says the rack end sits well inside both crossovers")
    check(abs(z_star_side_half_b.magnitude - 4.90) < 0.005, f"Checkpoint answer drifted: {z_star_side_half_b}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    b_str = fmt_length(b, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_px_str = fmt(f_px, precision=0)
    sigma_d_px_str = fmt(sigma_d_px, precision=1)
    z_near_str = fmt_length(z_near, unit=meter, precision=0)
    z_far_str = fmt_length(z_far, unit=meter, precision=0)
    sigma_z_near_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_near, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    sigma_z_far_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_far, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    c_ray_str = fmt_length(c_ray, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    naive_near_str = fmt_length(naive_near, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    naive_far_str = fmt_length(naive_far, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    db_str = fmt_length(db, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    z_thermal_str = fmt_length(z_thermal, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dz_thermal_str = fmt_length(dz_thermal, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    z_rack_str = fmt_length(z_rack.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    sigma_z_rack_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_rack, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    z_star_loc_str = fmt_length(z_star_loc, unit=meter, precision=0)
    z_star_side_str = fmt_length(z_star_side, unit=meter, precision=1)

    # Display arithmetic for nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall (magnitudes, LaTeX units)
    _fb = fmt(f_px * b.to(meter).magnitude, precision=0)  # f b in pixel-meters
    _sd = fmt(sigma_d_px, precision=1)
    _zn = fmt(z_near.to(meter).magnitude, precision=0)
    _zf = fmt(z_far.to(meter).magnitude, precision=0)
    _ratio = fmt((sigma_z_far / sigma_z_near).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude, precision=0)
    _loc = fmt(delta_loc.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)
    _side = fmt(side_clearance.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)
    sigma_rack_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\sigma_z = \frac{{z^2 \sigma_d}}{{f b}} = \frac{{({fmt(z_rack.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)}\ \text{{m}})^2 \times {_sd}\ \text{{px}}}}{{{f_px_str}\ \text{{px}} \times {fmt(b.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)}\ \text{{m}}}} = {fmt(sigma_z_rack.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad \frac{{\sigma_z({_zf}\ \text{{m}})}}{{\sigma_z({_zn}\ \text{{m}})}} = \frac{{{fmt(sigma_z_far.magnitude, precision=1)}}}{{{fmt(sigma_z_near.magnitude, precision=1)}}} = {_ratio}"
    )
    crossover_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"z^{{*}} = \sqrt{{\frac{{C\,f b}}{{\sigma_d}}}}: \quad \sqrt{{\frac{{{_loc}\ \text{{m}} \times {_fb}\ \text{{px}}\cdot\text{{m}}}}{{{_sd}\ \text{{px}}}}}} = {fmt(z_star_loc.magnitude, precision=0)}\ \text{{m}}, \quad \sqrt{{\frac{{{_side}\ \text{{m}} \times {_fb}\ \text{{px}}\cdot\text{{m}}}}{{{_sd}\ \text{{px}}}}}} = {fmt(z_star_side.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{m}}"
    )
```

To quantify the geometry, assume an illustrative stereo pair (the navigation camera alone recovers only the bearing ray of @eq-percep-bearing-ray) and ask how far down the aisle its depth error stays inside the stopping budget's allowances. Notebook \ref{nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall} evaluates @eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty on that rig, and @fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance plots the curve.

::: {#nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall .callout-notebook title="The stereo range wall"}

**Problem**: An illustrative stereo pair must place a rack upright for the base's clearance checks. How large is its one-standard-deviation depth scale at the rack end, and at what range does that scale alone consume the localization allowance and then the whole side clearance?

**Variables**:

* Baseline $b =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str`, focal length $f =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.f_px_str` px, and disparity standard deviation $\sigma_d =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_d_px_str` px over the tested range (Illustrative rig; the running machine carries no depth camera).
* Rack-end range $z =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.z_rack_str` (Illustrative).
* Allowances $C$: localization $\delta_{\text{loc}} =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.delta_loc_str` and side clearance `{python} StereoDepthError.side_clearance_str` (Illustrative; @tbl-01-machine-card).

**Math**:

*Depth scale.* At the rack end, and between the figure's two quoted ranges,
`{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_rack_math`

*Crossover ranges.* Setting $\sigma_z$ equal to an allowance $C$ and solving for range,
`{python} StereoDepthError.crossover_math`

*Sensitivity.* Five times the range costs twenty-five times the depth scale, so the crossovers move only with the square root of $f b / \sigma_d$.

**Result**: At the rack end, one standard deviation is `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_rack_str`. It equals $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_loc_str` and the whole side clearance at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_side_str`.

**Systems insight**: Stereo depth error is a range budget. This rig can support the rack-end decision, but a claim about an obstacle several meters down the aisle spends the stopping budget's $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ on one standard deviation alone, before any tail, bias, or timing term, so beyond a few meters the clearance claim must come from a range sensor whose error does not grow with $z^2$, or the speed must fall.

:::

The notebook's values are **one-standard-deviation scales**, not clearance insets or 99th-percentile bounds. A usable inset requires a tail quantile of the *full spatial residual*, calibrated on the intended sensor, range, texture, motion, and lighting conditions, with systematic bias and missed detections handled separately.

A pervasive trap in visual estimation is assuming that measurement errors follow a nominal Gaussian distribution where a $3\sigma$ gate bounds 99.7 percent of all errors. In physical vision, disparity estimation relies on matching pixel patches across stereo images. When scenes contain repetitive textures (such as corrugated warehouse siding), specular reflections from polished concrete floors, or partial occlusions along object silhouettes, correspondence matching produces catastrophic multimodal outliers rather than Gaussian scatter. Some fraction of stereo returns are then complete mismatch outliers lying many standard deviations from the true surface, and that fraction depends on the scene's texture, lighting, and the matcher, so it must be measured on residuals from the deployment's own scenes rather than assumed. Relying on Gaussian $3\sigma$ bounds without robust loss formulations (such as Huber or Tukey loss) or heavy-tailed empirical quantile validation allows these gross outliers to distort the state estimate, compromising physical clearance. A `{python} StereoDepthError.c_ray_str` clearance kept along the viewing ray to an obstacle therefore cannot be widened to a valid inset of `{python} StereoDepthError.naive_near_str` or `{python} StereoDepthError.naive_far_str` merely by adding one $\sigma_z$. Speed must be reduced or the proposal refused whenever the validated range-error and stopping margins do not fit.

### Clearance inset margins and transform chain propagation

Spatial error extends beyond the sensor optical frame. To govern motion, the estimated point must propagate through coordinate transformations to the robot base frame and the end effector. The mechanics of rigid body transformations\index{Rigid body transformations} and SE(3) kinematic frame composition\index{SE(3) kinematics} are standard results treated by Craig [@craig2005introduction] as well as @lynch2017modern. Each link in this transform chain contributes scale errors, mounting calibration drift, joint encoder quantization, and mechanical compliance under load (such as a robot arm sagging slightly under gravity). As the reference-frame property of @sec-perception-handoff showed, a small angular twist at the sensor mount grows linearly with range. If the navigation camera's extrinsic calibration shifts by $\theta =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_ext_str` rad against the chassis, the lateral error $\delta x \approx z\theta$ at $z =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.z_ext_str` is `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dx_ext_str`, equal in size to the whole `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.delta_loc_str` localization allowance $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ that the stopping budget holds along the direction of travel. The comparison is one of scale, not allocation. The allowance carries small validated residuals, such as the clock-conversion travel of @sec-perception-observation-contract, and a shift that matches it alone is a calibration failure the consumer must refuse through the calibration validity check rather than absorb. When combined with quadratic depth uncertainty, the total spatial error vector $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}$ at long range is dominated by depth along the optical axis and angular lever-arm effects orthogonal to it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Spatial covariance envelopes inflate the forward-invariant safety barrier sets derived in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

Every physical safety barrier operates by defending a geometric boundary around the machine. For position error vector $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}$, the triangle inequality gives a conservative relation between nominal and true clearance:
$$C_{\text{true}} \ge C_{\text{nominal}} - \|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}\|$$
For a validated 99th-percentile norm-error quantile, the permission path can hold the estimate at a clearance inset $C_{\text{inset}}$ (@eq-percep-clearance-inset):
$$C_{\text{inset}} = C_{\text{safe}} + \|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}\|_{P_{99}}$$ {#eq-percep-clearance-inset}
Here $C_{\text{safe}}$ is the physical clearance the motion must keep, such as the base's side clearance, and the quantile must come from a specified, checked residual distribution for the full spatial error, including calibration bias. Even then it leaves a 1 percent tail under the test distribution; only a justified hard bound on the relevant error, a feasible stopping path, and a permission response within the remaining delay budget would close it.

::: {#dfn-perception-clearance-inset .callout-definition title="Clearance inset"}

***Clearance inset***\index{Clearance inset!definition} ($C_{\text{inset}}$) is the separation a consumer holds between an estimated obstacle position and the machine's envelope so that the true obstacle stays at least the required physical clearance away, except with a stated tail probability measured under the conditions of use.

1.  **Significance**: The inset converts measured spatial error into clearance that the motion gives up (@eq-percep-clearance-inset). Every millimeter of qualified error widens the region the permission path treats as occupied, so the planner must slow or route farther away. On the illustrative stereo rig, one standard deviation of depth error alone equals the base's `{python} StereoDepthError.side_clearance_str` side clearance at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_side_str`, so there the inset would double the clearance even if the residual tail were no wider than one standard deviation.
2.  **Distinction**: A covariance describes the second moments of the error an estimator believes it has; the inset rests on residuals measured against ground truth, so it includes the bias and heavy tail that the covariance omits. A 99th-percentile inset is also not a hard bound: it leaves 1 percent of residuals outside, which only a justified bound on the error or a feasible stop within the remaining delay budget can close.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a reported covariance, or a depth network's predicted spread, sets the inset. Neither is measured against ground truth, so neither contains the calibration bias and mismatch outliers that the residual campaign of @sec-perception-qualifying-error captures.

:::

@Fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance shows how stereo's growing depth-error scale can require a larger inset at longer range.

::: {#fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Depth error scale and clearance inset**: (a) For the illustrative stereo rig, the one-standard-deviation depth scale grows with squared range, from `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_near_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_near_str` to `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_far_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_far_str`; the gray band is the machine LiDAR's datasheet range precision, which stays flat beyond 1 m. (b) A schematic error distribution along the viewing ray. Holding the estimate at $C_{\text{inset}} = C_{\text{safe}} + \|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\|_{P_{99}}$ keeps the true surface beyond $C_{\text{safe}}$ except in the shaded residual tail, which the quantile leaves and which bias can enlarge." fig-alt="Two panels. Left: a line plot of one-sigma depth error in millimeters against range in meters, a curve rising quadratically with two marked points at 2 and 10 meters, above a flat gray band for the LiDAR precision. Right: a schematic bell-shaped distribution with heavy tails along a distance axis with ticks for body, C safe, and C inset; the estimate sits at the dashed C inset line, an arrow between C safe and C inset is labeled with the 99th-percentile error norm, and the small part of the distribution closer than C safe is shaded red and labeled residual tail and bias."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-perception-depth-clearance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DEPTH ERROR SCALE AND CLEARANCE INSET (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance in
# │          @sec-perception-error-clearance.
# │
# │ Goal:    Contrast a stereo depth scale that grows with squared range with
# │          the machine LiDAR's flat datasheet precision, then show what a
# │          validated quantile inset buys and what it leaves.
# │ Show:    (a) sigma_z(z) for the illustrative stereo rig with its two quoted
# │          points, and the OS1-64 precision band; (b) a schematic error
# │          density along the viewing ray with C_safe, the P99 inset, and the
# │          residual tail.
# │ How:     (a) reads StereoDepthError and LidarSweep (no literals); (b) is a
# │          schematic with symbolic ticks only (no plotted numbers).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

SDE, LS = StereoDepthError, LidarSweep
PETROL, INK, SOFT, PALE = "#007A87", "#1A202C", "#4A5568", "#A0AEC0"
PINE, CRIMSON = "#1A4D3E", "#A51C30"  # structural, consequence (theme-colors.tex)

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
k_mm_per_m2 = (SDE.sigma_d_px / (SDE.f_px * SDE.b)).to(ureg.millimeter / meter**2).magnitude  # category: derived
z_far_m = SDE.z_far.to(meter).magnitude
z_near_m = SDE.z_near.to(meter).magnitude
lid_lo = LS.sigma_r_min.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude  # category: datasheet
lid_hi = LS.sigma_r_max.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude  # category: datasheet

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
z = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2 * z_far_m, 200)
sig = k_mm_per_m2 * z**2

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2 - SDE.sigma_z_far.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Plotted stereo curve must pass through sigma_z_far.")
check(abs(k_mm_per_m2 * z_near_m**2 - SDE.sigma_z_near.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Plotted stereo curve must pass through sigma_z_near.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.7), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.0, 1.15], wspace=0.28))

# (a) depth error scale
ax.axhspan(lid_lo, lid_hi, xmin=1.0 / (1.2 * z_far_m), color=PALE, alpha=0.45, lw=0)
ax.text(
    1.2 * z_far_m * 0.98,
    lid_hi + 10,
    f"LiDAR $\\sigma_R$, {LS.sigma_r_min_str} to {LS.sigma_r_max_str}",
    ha="right",
    va="bottom",
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=SOFT,
)
ax.plot(z, sig, color=PETROL, lw=1.8)
for zz, s_str in ((z_near_m, SDE.sigma_z_near_str), (z_far_m, SDE.sigma_z_far_str)):
    ax.plot([zz], [k_mm_per_m2 * zz**2], "o", color=PETROL, ms=4)
ax.annotate(
    f"{SDE.sigma_z_far_str} at {SDE.z_far_str}",
    xy=(z_far_m, k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2),
    xytext=(z_far_m * 0.18, k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2 * 1.05),
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=PETROL,
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PALE, lw=0.6),
)
ax.annotate(
    f"{SDE.sigma_z_near_str} at {SDE.z_near_str}",
    xy=(z_near_m, k_mm_per_m2 * z_near_m**2),
    xytext=(z_near_m * 0.55, k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2 * 0.42),
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=PETROL,
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PALE, lw=0.6),
)
ax.text(z_far_m * 0.62, k_mm_per_m2 * (z_far_m * 1.1) ** 2, r"stereo $\sigma_z \propto z^2$", fontsize=8, color=PETROL, ha="right", va="center")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.2 * z_far_m)
ax.set_ylim(0, k_mm_per_m2 * (1.2 * z_far_m) ** 2 * 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel("range $z$ (m)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("one-sigma depth error (mm)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("(a)", fontsize=9, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)

# (b) schematic: error density along the viewing ray, heavy tailed
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 600)
c_safe, c_inset = 3.4, 6.0
dens = (1 + ((x - c_inset) / 0.8) ** 2 / 2.0) ** (-1.5)
bx.fill_between(x, 0, dens, where=x >= c_safe, color=PETROL, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
bx.fill_between(x, 0, dens, where=x <= c_safe, color=CRIMSON, alpha=0.35, lw=0)
bx.plot(x, dens, color=PETROL, lw=1.3)
bx.axvline(c_safe, color=PINE, lw=1.2)
bx.axvline(c_inset, color=PINE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
bx.text(c_inset + 0.1, 1.1, "estimate held\nat the inset", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5, color=SOFT)
bx.annotate("", xy=(c_safe, 0.86), xytext=(c_inset, 0.86), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=PINE, lw=0.9))
bx.text((c_safe + c_inset) / 2, 0.9, "$\\|\\,\\epsilon\\,\\|_{P_{99}}$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=PINE)
bx.annotate("", xy=(0, 0.62), xytext=(c_safe, 0.62), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=PINE, lw=0.9))
bx.text(c_safe / 2, 0.66, "$C_{\\mathrm{safe}}$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=PINE)
bx.annotate(
    "residual tail\nand bias",
    xy=(c_safe - 0.5, 0.05),
    xytext=(c_safe - 0.4, 0.34),
    ha="right",
    va="center",
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=CRIMSON,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=CRIMSON, lw=0.6),
)
bx.set_xticks([0, c_safe, c_inset])
bx.set_xticklabels(["body", "$C_{\\mathrm{safe}}$", "$C_{\\mathrm{inset}}$"], fontsize=8)
bx.set_yticks([])
bx.set_xlim(0, 10)
bx.set_ylim(0, 1.3)
bx.set_xlabel("distance along the viewing ray", fontsize=8.5)
bx.grid(False)
bx.set_title("(b)", fontsize=9, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
for s in ("top", "right", "left"):
    bx.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

:::

Because clearance depends on propagated error, downstream planners and the permission path cannot consume raw coordinate tuples. A covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ alone does not say whether a $10\text{ mm}$ or $500\text{ mm}$ clearance inset is warranted; that takes an independently validated tail or hard bound.

When spatial error is qualified, the permission path can expand the clearance inset, trading speed or workspace for separation. Downstream deterministic safety filters (such as the Control Barrier Functions derived in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission) enforce forward invariance against this expanded boundary $C_{\text{inset}}$, preserving the physical clearance buffer against sensing and calibration error. A textureless wall, glare, or lost calibration can invalidate that qualification without making a numerical variance literally infinite. The permission path must then refuse motion that depends on the affected claim and select a feasible fallback.

On every frame the producer builds a spatial claim in a fixed order, and any step can end it. It first converts the capture timestamp to the consumer's clock with a bounded synchronization error and computes $t_{\text{age}}$; if age plus clock uncertainty exceeds the refusal threshold, it marks the observation stale, and proposals that need it are refused. At admission and subsequent ticks, the permission path computes the current evidence age from capture time; the dispatch threshold is not the current-age threshold (@sec-perception-observation-contract). For a fresh observation, the producer unprojects each pixel measurement into optical coordinates with a sensor covariance,[^fn-covariance-unprojection-depth] and carries point and covariance into the body frame by first-order SE(3) error propagation\index{SE(3) kinematics!error propagation} through the calibrated extrinsics at capture. A consumer that predicts forward must attach its motion-model uncertainty without changing the evidence epoch. Validated residuals, including bias, then set the inset radius, and when no valid bound remains, the affected motion is refused. What leaves perception is a claim $(\mathbf{p}_{\text{body}}, \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{body}}, C_{\text{inset}}, t_{\text{age}})$, not a bare coordinate.

[^fn-covariance-unprojection-depth]: **Covariance Propagation**\index{Mathematics!covariance propagation}: First-order propagation maps measurement covariance to $\mathbf{\Sigma}_c = \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}}\mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}^\top$ in the optical frame and then to $\mathbf{\Sigma}_b = \mathbf{R}_{bc}\mathbf{\Sigma}_c\mathbf{R}_{bc}^\top + \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}}$ in the body frame, where the extrinsic term is what a mount shift adds. Its largest eigenvalue gives the principal variance scale, which for stereo points lies along the viewing ray; see @sec-appendix-systems-vision.

That claim describes one measurement at one instant, and perception's responsibility ends with it. Keeping the rack-end range current between sweeps, fusing the LiDAR with a second sensor, joining detections into tracks, and applying a late measurement at its capture epoch are estimation over time. @Sec-perception-state-estimation develops them as the foundation of spatial memory, and every one of them consumes the dated, framed, error-qualified claim built here. What perception must still supply is evidence that the claimed error was measured.

### Qualifying the claimed error {#sec-perception-qualifying-error}

The record of @sec-perception-observation-contract asks for a tail quantile that sets the clearance inset and a measured clock-conversion bound. Each has a standard measurement procedure. Whether a reported covariance matches the actual error is tested with statistics that need an estimator's prediction, so that test is developed with the estimator (@sec-memory-estimator-consistency).

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-error-qualification
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TAIL-QUANTILE AND CLOCK-DRIFT QUALIFICATION NUMBERS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-perception-qualifying-error.
# │
# │ Goal:    Give the conformal rank for a 99th-percentile bound and the drift
# │          of a free-running sensor clock between syncs.
# │ Show:    at least 99 residuals for a 1 percent bound; with 1,000, the 991st
# │          smallest (10th largest); 10 us of drift.
# │ How:     split-conformal rank ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha)); Ouster OS1 Rev7
# │          internal clock drift (10 ppm) over a chosen 1 s sync interval.
# │          The covariance-consistency bands moved with the estimator to
# │          @sec-memory-estimator-consistency.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ErrorQualification:
    """Sample sizes for a clearance-inset quantile and the clock-drift bound."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    alpha = 0.01  # category: chosen (tail mass for the clearance inset)
    n_resid = 1000  # category: chosen (calibration residuals)
    drift_ppm = RM.lidar.internal_clock_drift.to(ureg.ppm).magnitude  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 internal clock drift)
    t_sync = 1.0 * second  # category: chosen (sync interval)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_min = math.ceil((1 - alpha) / alpha)
    k_rank = math.ceil((n_resid + 1) * (1 - alpha))
    k_from_top = n_resid - k_rank + 1
    drift = (drift_ppm * 1e-6 * t_sync).to(microsecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_min == 99, f"Unexpected minimum calibration size: {n_min}")
    check(k_rank == 991 and k_from_top == 10, f"Unexpected conformal rank: {k_rank}")
    check(abs(drift.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected clock drift: {drift}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_pct_str = fmt_percent(alpha, precision=0)
    n_min_str = fmt_int(n_min)
    n_resid_str = fmt_int(n_resid, commas=True)
    k_rank_str = fmt_int(k_rank)
    k_from_top_str = fmt_int(k_from_top)
    drift_ppm_str = fmt(drift_ppm, precision=0)
    t_sync_str = fmt(t_sync.to(second).magnitude, precision=0)
    drift_str = fmt_latency(drift, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
```

**What sets the inset?** The clearance inset of @eq-percep-clearance-inset needs a 99th-percentile bound on the residual norm under the intended conditions, not a covariance. The most direct procedure is empirical. Collect $n$ residual norms against ground truth, sort them, and take the $k$-th smallest with $k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$. This split-conformal rule guarantees that a new residual falls at or below the bound with probability at least $1 - \alpha$ when calibration and deployment residuals are exchangeable [@angelopoulos2023gentle]. For $\alpha =$ `{python} ErrorQualification.alpha_pct_str` percent the rule needs at least `{python} ErrorQualification.n_min_str` residuals, and with exactly that many it returns the largest one observed. With `{python} ErrorQualification.n_resid_str` residuals it returns the `{python} ErrorQualification.k_rank_str`st smallest, the `{python} ErrorQualification.k_from_top_str`th largest. The guarantee is marginal over the calibration conditions. A new floor finish, a lighting change, or a recalibration breaks exchangeability, and the campaign that collects the residuals is sized by the reasoning of @sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim. Because the residuals are measured against ground truth, they include the sensor's bias, which the covariance does not.

**How good is the clock?** The bound $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ in the record is measured, not assumed. In a PTP exchange the master sends a Sync message at $t_1$ that the device receives at $t_2$, and the device sends a Delay_Req at $t_3$ that the master receives at $t_4$. The protocol estimates the device's clock offset as $\theta = \left[(t_2 - t_1) - (t_4 - t_3)\right]/2$ and the mean path delay as $\left[(t_2 - t_1) + (t_4 - t_3)\right]/2$ [@ieee15882019]. The estimate assumes the two directions take equal time. A path asymmetry $\Delta$ shifts $\theta$ by $\Delta/2$ without any symptom in the exchange, which is why stamping at the network interface in hardware, rather than in software, matters. Between exchanges the local oscillator drifts. The OS1-64's free-running clock is specified at `{python} ErrorQualification.drift_ppm_str` ppm [@ouster2025os1], which over a `{python} ErrorQualification.t_sync_str` s sync interval accumulates `{python} ErrorQualification.drift_str`. The qualified bound is the measured tail of the servo's reported offset over a qualification run, plus the asymmetry bound, plus the drift between corrections. For a hardware-triggered camera the same bound comes from timing the trigger edge against the IMU latch with a logic analyzer. Until those measurements exist, the clock-conversion bound in the navigation camera's record remains illustrative, and the LiDAR's datasheet promises only `{python} LidarAge.eps_ptp_str`.

### Learned depth as a measurement

Learned models add two things to the metric claims of this section: a label for what occupies a region, and a depth estimate from a camera that by itself measures only bearing. Lifting labeled detections into a persistent, object-centric scene graph carries state across frames, and @sec-memory-hierarchical-scene-graphs builds and maintains that graph. Perception has a narrower question to settle, whether a learned depth estimate may enter a clearance claim at all. The semantic layer identifies candidate objects and contacts; the metric layer must still establish their geometry. Point clouds supply measured surface samples, and missing samples do not establish free space. The persistent representations that retain geometric evidence (@sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps; @sec-appendix-ml-voxels and @sec-appendix-ml-3dgs give their update equations) do not change an observation's capture time or turn a learned score into an error bound.

Lifting 2D pixel features into 3D metric space requires combining 2D token embeddings with per-pixel depth distributions. In deep monocular depth networks (such as Depth Anything, MiDaS, or metric depth transformers), models predict dense depth maps from monocular cues. However, single-view depth estimation is inherently ill-posed due to projective scale ambiguity: an infinite family of physical 3D objects with different scales and distances project to identical pixel arrays. Relative-depth models may output scale- or affine-ambiguous predictions, whose conversion to metric depth requires calibration, represented here by $z_{\text{metric}} = s \cdot z_{\text{pred}} + t$ when the model uses that parameterization. Metric-trained heads can directly predict depth in meters, but their units do not certify their error. Either kind of model requires residual validation and can fail silently on unusual geometries, novel textures, or optical illusions (such as a 2D photograph printed on a flat surface).

In bird's-eye-view (BEV) architectures such as Lift-Splat-Shoot [@philion2020lift] (developed in @sec-appendix-ml-bev-lifting), the network predicts a categorical probability distribution over discrete depth bins along each viewing ray. Each 2D feature token is cast outward along its optical sightline ray and 'splatted' into discrete 3D spatial voxel cells weighted by these predicted depth probabilities, transforming disembodied image embeddings into an explicit 3D volumetric representation. The resulting spatial uncertainty ellipsoid deforms non-linearly under perspective unprojection through the unprojection Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_{\text{cartesian}}}{\partial [u, v, z]^\top}$ (@eq-percep-unproj-covariance):
$$\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{cartesian}} = \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ray}} \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}^\top$$ {#eq-percep-unproj-covariance}
While transverse spatial standard deviation expands linearly with range ($\sigma_\perp \approx \frac{z}{f} \sigma_{\text{px}}$), stereo radial depth standard deviation expands quadratically ($\sigma_z \approx \frac{z^2}{f b} \sigma_d$). This perspective unprojection transforms near-field circular uncertainty disks into highly eccentric, needle-shaped ellipsoids oriented along the camera's sightline, with extreme radial dispersion at long ranges that must be bound before downstream safety filters can certify clearance.

Because the depth-bin distributions produced by learned lifting stages are uncalibrated model scores rather than certified metric error bounds, the clearance inset of @eq-percep-clearance-inset cannot rest on learned depth alone. Downstream safety enforcers require continuous validation against calibrated active ranging sensors or stereo disparity.

::: {#psp-perception-metric-veto-invariant .callout-perspective title="The metric veto invariant"}
**Safety is an invariant of metric clearance, not semantic understanding.** When a slow 2 Hz vision-language foundation model classifies a pathway as "clear aisle" or dismisses an object as a harmless shadow, but a fast 60 Hz depth sensor or occupancy grid (@sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps) detects a physical obstacle return within the stopping envelope, the permission path must honor the qualified occupied-region evidence rather than let semantic confidence erase it. The permission path halts or slows the machine regardless of the semantic model's high confidence. Semantic models propose high-level task goals; qualified metric sensing supplies clearance evidence to the permission path. Neither sensor pipeline itself owns actuator authority.
:::

::: {#chk-percep-clearance-inset .callout-checkpoint title="Spatial error and the clearance inset"}

A spatial claim is spent from the same clearance as its age, and its error must be measured before it is charged.

- [ ] **Quadratic depth error**: Can you explain why stereo depth error grows with the square of range while a pulsed LiDAR's range precision stays roughly flat?
- [ ] **Baseline estimate**: If the illustrative rig's `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str` baseline were halved, at what range would one standard deviation of depth error reach the `{python} StereoDepthError.side_clearance_str` side clearance, compared with `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_side_str` now?
- [ ] **Covariance vs. clearance inset**: Can you explain why a residual quantile measured against ground truth, not a reported covariance, sets $C_{\text{inset}}$, and what that quantile still leaves uncovered?
- [ ] **Learned depth vs. metric evidence**: Can you explain why a depth network's predicted spread cannot enter a clearance claim until its residuals are validated, and why qualified metric evidence overrides a semantic label that calls a return a shadow?

:::

Every bound in this section, metric, learned, or temporal, assumes that the sensor behaves as calibrated. Propagation bounds the error of a sensor working as modeled; it says nothing about a sensor that has stopped working that way while still delivering frames at its nominal rate.

## Perception Failure Modes and Sensor Degradation {#sec-perception-failure-modes}

The navigation camera can fail in two ways that look nothing alike to its consumer. If its serializer link loses lock, the driver raises an error and the frame never arrives. If light through an open dock door saturates the lens as the base turns into an aisle, the camera delivers a complete frame at its nominal rate in which the rack end is a patch of saturated white. Perception failures divide along exactly this line into two operational classes. **Detectable faults**\index{Detectable faults} occur when the physical sensor or the communication transport reports an explicit error condition. A serializer-deserializer link drops a lock (losing clock synchronization), a cyclical redundancy check detects a corrupted payload, a frame buffer overflows, or a transport bus times out. These failures are straightforward to handle since the hardware driver asserts an error flag at the ingestion boundary. Downstream consumers register the missing frame and invalidate stale state estimates, and once the evidence age exceeds its budget the permission path refuses and moves the machine to a validated fallback. In contrast, **silent failures**\index{Silent failure!definition} occur when the sensor hardware and transport pipeline function without error, delivering a fully populated, structurally valid tensor whose numerical values misrepresent the physical world.

Physical degradation of the optical channel is a common source of silent error. When direct sunlight enters an optical aperture, incident photons exceed the physical charge capacity (the "full-well capacity") of the CMOS photodiodes, clamping pixel intensities at their maximum quantization limit (clipping the image to pure white) across large patches of the array. This **dynamic range saturation**\index{Dynamic range saturation} destroys local spatial gradients. Feature extractors, optical flow estimators, and disparity matching algorithms fail because mathematical optimization on a uniform flat field yields zero information, yet the driver emits a valid frame at nominal line rate. Low-light environments introduce the opposite failure mode. As ambient illumination drops, the discrete, random arrival of individual photons (**photon shot noise**\index{Photon shot noise}) and the intrinsic electrical fluctuations of the sensor's amplifier (**sensor read noise**\index{Sensor read noise}) dominate the measurement. The signal-to-noise ratio collapses, causing downstream neural networks to extract geometric features from random noise fluctuations rather than physical scene boundaries. Environmental contaminants on the protective lens or dome window (such as water droplets, airborne dust, or mud splatters) act as irregular refractive elements and optical low-pass filters. They attenuate contrast, distort spatial geometry, and obscure obstacles while the transport bus continues to operate without asserting a single fault flag.

Timing and transport anomalies can also corrupt an observation silently. If an unshielded physical interface experiences electromagnetic interference, deserializer bit slips (where the hardware drops or duplicates a bit, misaligning the entire subsequent data stream) can alter payload semantics without invalidating standard packet lengths. More dangerous than a lost packet, because nothing flags it, is an observation delivered with a timestamp that misreports its true capture epoch. If an image sensor captures photons at epoch $t_0$, but a late interrupt handler or an unsynchronized system clock timestamps the resulting memory buffer at $t_0 + \delta t$, the downstream state estimator integrates spatial features under an incorrect body pose. Consider a machine traveling with instantaneous velocity $v$ and linear acceleration $a$ along a given trajectory. When perception suffers an undetected timing desynchronization $\delta t$, the state estimator assigns the detected position of an obstacle to the body coordinates at $t_0 + \delta t$ rather than $t_0$. Over the unmodeled time interval $\delta t$, the physical state estimation error $\Delta p$ between the asserted position and the true position is governed by the kinematic drift relation (@eq-percep-kinematic-drift):
$$\Delta p = v \cdot \delta t + \frac{1}{2} a \cdot (\delta t)^2$$ {#eq-percep-kinematic-drift}

The arrival stamp of @sec-perception-handoff is a silent desynchronization of exactly this kind. At a constant drive speed the acceleration term vanishes, leaving the $v\,\tau_{\text{recv}}$ offset sized there, and nothing raises a fault flag. @Sec-perception-state-estimation follows such a measurement into an estimator, which moves its estimate by nearly the full offset while the reported variance stays unchanged. A missing frame causes a known information loss that a state observer or policy can handle by expanding its uncertainty covariance, while a frame that arrives on time with a corrupt timestamp contracts the uncertainty around an incorrect spatial state, so the machine plans toward an obstacle it believes it has already cleared.

Defending against silent failure requires dedicated runtime health monitors at the sensor ingestion boundary. A pixel intensity histogram monitor measures the distribution of raw digitized values immediately after direct memory access transfer, identifying over-exposure saturation when values concentrate at the maximum bit depth or identifying lens occlusion when spatial variance drops below an empirical noise floor. A hardware watchdog timer tracks inter-arrival times across the direct memory access channel, flagging transport jitter when inter-frame intervals exceed $T_{\text{nominal}} + 3\sigma_{\text{jitter}}$. Higher up the stack, an optical flow plausibility monitor compares computed pixel displacement vectors against the physical velocity envelope of the body, rejecting observations that imply accelerations beyond mechanical capability. In multi-modal configurations, a cross-sensor consistency check compares high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) inertial measurement unit integrations against visual odometry. If the visual pipeline reports that the machine is stationary while the gravity-compensated inertial estimate indicates sustained $2.0\text{ m/s}^2$ linear acceleration, the monitor can flag a discrepancy once attitude, bias, timing, and measurement uncertainty are accounted for.

Every runtime health monitor sees the world only through what the transducer reported at the causal boundary of @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, so a single sensing channel cannot validate its own semantic interpretations. A camera assembly with clean optics, balanced exposure, jitter-free transport, and synchronized microsecond clocking can still present an observation that leads a learned model to hallucinate a clear path or ignore an obstacle. Because deep vision models project high-dimensional inputs through complex non-linear manifolds, in-distribution optical anomalies (such as a high-contrast shadow across an aisle, a person printed on a carton, or specular glare from shrink-wrap or a wet floor) generate plausible pixel statistics, valid optical flow fields, and high model confidence. A single-sensor monitor evaluates whether the data collection process operated within nominal limits, not whether the inferred semantics match physical reality. A second modality, such as lidar or radar, can corroborate some optical claims when its coverage and failure dependence have been checked. A separately validated permission path can enforce clearance only within its sensing, model, timing, and actuator assumptions; neither route establishes unrestricted semantic truth.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-degraded-optics
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FOG CONTRAST RANGE AND WRIST-CAMERA MOTION TRAVEL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The atmospheric-scattering and motion-blur items of
# │          the environmental-degradation subsection.
# │
# │ Goal:    Range at which dense fog drops contrast to the 0.05 threshold,
# │          and camera-center travel during one wrist-camera exposure.
# │ Show:    ln(1/0.05) / 0.05 m^-1 = 60 m; 0.5 m x 3 rad/s x 5 ms = 7.5 mm.
# │ How:     Koschmieder C = C0 exp(-beta d); dx = r omega t_exp with the
# │          registry exposure of the machine's wrist camera (Sony IMX296).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class DegradedOptics:
    """Fog contrast range and wrist-camera travel within one exposure."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    beta_fog = 0.05 / meter  # category: illustrative (dense-fog extinction coefficient)
    eps_contrast = 0.05  # category: standard (5 percent contrast threshold of meteorological optical range)
    t_exp = RM.wrist_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (registry: IMX296 configured exposure)
    r_arm = 0.5 * meter  # category: illustrative (lever arm from rotation axis to camera)
    omega = 3.0 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (sweep angular rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_fog = (math.log(1 / eps_contrast) / beta_fog).to(meter)
    dx_blur = (r_arm * omega.to(1 / second).magnitude / second * t_exp).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(d_fog.magnitude - 59.9) < 0.1, f"Unexpected fog range: {d_fog}")
    check(RM.wrist_camera.shutter_type == "global", "The wrist camera is the global-shutter IMX296.")
    check(abs(t_exp.magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected wrist exposure: {t_exp}")
    check(abs(dx_blur.magnitude - 7.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected blur travel: {dx_blur}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    beta_fog_str = fmt(beta_fog.to(1 / meter).magnitude, precision=2)
    eps_contrast_str = fmt(eps_contrast, precision=2)
    d_fog_str = fmt_length(round(d_fog.magnitude) * meter, unit=meter, precision=0)  # 59.9 m shown to the meter
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    r_arm_str = fmt_length(r_arm, unit=meter, precision=1)
    omega_str = fmt(omega.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=0)
    dx_blur_str = fmt_length(dx_blur, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
```

### Environmental degradation under precipitation, fog, and lens flare

Physical environments continuously degrade sensory transmission across optical, near-infrared, and radio channels. A perception architecture operating across factory yards, loading docks, or public roadways must anticipate how weather and illumination alter signal-to-noise ratios without asserting hardware error flags.

**Optical cameras in atmospheric scattering and glare**: Suspended airborne aerosol particles in fog, mist, and smoke ($1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{m}$ diameter) scatter visible wavelengths ($\lambda \approx 400\text{--}700\,\text{nm}$) under Mie scattering physics. Scene radiance attenuates exponentially across distance according to Koschmieder's law:
$$C(d) = C_0 \, e^{-\beta_{\text{atm}} d}$$
where $C_0$ is intrinsic object contrast, $d$ is metric range, and $\beta_{\text{atm}}$ is the atmospheric extinction coefficient. In dense fog ($\beta_{\text{atm}} \approx$ `{python} DegradedOptics.beta_fog_str`$\,\text{m}^{-1}$, an illustrative value), apparent contrast decays below the `{python} DegradedOptics.eps_contrast_str` perceptual detection threshold within `{python} DegradedOptics.d_fog_str`. High-frequency edge gradients dissolve into uniform background luminance, preventing convolutional and transformer backbones from forming valid feature embeddings. Airborne rain introduces high-velocity streak noise across frames, while droplets impacting the protective lens act as irregular refractive microlenses. Each droplet deflects incoming rays, creating severe localized geometric distortion, optical blur, and false object silhouettes.

**High angular velocity motion blur and MTF collapse**:[^fn-mtf-optical-blur] During a yaw rotation or manipulator sweep, a camera center at lever arm $r$ travels a tangential distance set by angular rate $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ and exposure duration:
$$\Delta x_{\text{rot}} = r \cdot \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| \cdot t_{\text{exp}}$$
For the machine's global-shutter wrist camera at its configured `{python} DegradedOptics.t_exp_str` exposure, swept at an illustrative $\omega =$ `{python} DegradedOptics.omega_str` rad/s on an illustrative lever arm $r =$ `{python} DegradedOptics.r_arm_str`, this travel scale is $\Delta x \approx$ `{python} DegradedOptics.dx_blur_str`. It is not an image-plane blur width. Scene depth and camera projection determine the image motion due to translation, while attitude change also moves image features even without camera-center translation. Blur can attenuate the gradients used by feature matching, visual odometry, and learned perception; its effect on tracking and learned features requires evaluation over the intended motion and exposure range.

[^fn-mtf-optical-blur]: **Modulation Transfer Function (MTF)**: The fraction of scene contrast an imaging chain passes at each spatial frequency. A uniform blur of length $L$ in the image multiplies it by a sinc that falls to zero at a period of $L$, so detail finer than the blur is erased rather than dimmed, and no network downstream can restore what the exposure removed. \index{Modulation transfer function!motion blur}

**High Dynamic Range (HDR) saturation and blooming**: Auto-exposure handles a change of illumination between scenes, from a shaded aisle to a sunlit yard, by changing $t_{\text{exp}}$ from frame to frame. It cannot handle contrast within one frame. When a robot in a dim aisle faces an open, sunlit loading dock, one exposure must serve both regions, and a setting long enough to resolve the aisle lets the dock's photon flux exceed each photodiode's full-well charge capacity, driving those pixels into deep saturation. HDR sensors extend the range by combining several exposures or several pixel sensitivities, which raises a timing question the record must answer: when the exposures are staggered, each region of the merged image carries a different exposure midpoint, so the capture epoch must name which exposure it dates. Excess photo-generated electrons overflow past barrier implants into adjacent pixel wells (**charge blooming**), wiping out entire array regions into uniform saturated white ($255$). Internal reflections between lens elements create veiling glare and flare streaks, eliminating the spatial contrast required for disparity matching and optical flow.

**LiDAR in airborne particulates, retroreflector blooming, and specular surfaces**: Pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR, at silicon-band near-infrared wavelengths and at $1{,}550\,\text{nm}$ alike, suffers three distinct physical failure mechanisms in industrial and outdoor operation:

1. *Aerosol backscatter clutter*: Emitted laser pulses strike suspended fog droplets and dust particulates, scattering optical power directly back into the receiver during the initial nanoseconds of flight. This generates dense near-field point clutter, often appearing as a solid "phantom wall" within $0.5\text{--}3.0\,\text{meters}$ of the aperture. Downstream spatial clustering algorithms interpret these returns as immediate collision obstacles, triggering false emergency stops. Concurrently, forward beam attenuation depletes pulse energy and shortens effective range; how much depends on the extinction coefficient of the rain or fog and on the target's reflectivity, so the shortened range must be measured for the sensor under the conditions it is qualified for.
2. *Retroreflector detector blooming and range walk*: High-visibility safety vests, barcode placards, and vehicle license plates incorporate retroreflective prismatic surfaces designed to return incoming light directly along the emission axis, far more of it than a diffuse surface returns. The strong pulse causes two distinct errors. **Range walk**\index{LiDAR!range walk} is a timing error in the receiver's avalanche photodiodes (APDs) or single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs): a leading-edge discriminator fires when the return crosses a fixed threshold, and a strong, fast-rising pulse crosses it earlier than a weak one, so the range to the vest reads short by an amount that depends on the return's amplitude and that the receiver's intensity correction removes only while the pre-amplifier stays unsaturated. **Blooming** is a spatial error: stray light and electrical crosstalk from the saturating return register in neighboring beams and pixels, surrounding the retroreflector with a halo of phantom points where nothing stands. The machine's datasheet already separates the two cases by quoting a looser accuracy for retroreflective targets than for diffuse ones [@ouster2025os1].
3. *Specular surfaces and non-Lambertian forward bounce*: Triangulation sensors, structured light, and LiDAR rely on the physical assumption of diffuse Lambertian scattering. Specular surfaces—including polished warehouse concrete floors, shrink-wrapped palletized freight, metallic shelving, and architectural glass—violate this assumption. Emitted laser pulses undergo specular reflection, leaving at an angle from the surface normal equal to the angle of incidence ($\theta_r = \theta_i$) and so directing light away from the sensor. On wet floors, this creates artificial zero-return dropouts ("puddle black holes"); on glass walls or metal panels, it induces multi-bounce reflections, projecting phantom obstacle points meters behind walls or beneath the floor.

**FMCW radar all-weather resilience**: Operating at $76\text{--}81\,\text{GHz}$, FMCW millimeter-wave radar features a wavelength of $\lambda \approx 3.9\,\text{mm}$—roughly 4,000 times larger than optical laser pulses and substantially larger than fog aerosol droplets ($1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{m}$). Scattering by airborne particles follows Rayleigh scattering physics, where the particle scattering cross-section $\sigma_s$ scales inversely with the fourth power of wavelength:
$$\sigma_s \propto \frac{d_{\text{droplet}}^6}{\lambda^4}$$
This wavelength dependence explains radar's reduced sensitivity to small airborne particles in the Rayleigh regime; it does not establish immunity to weather. Ground reflections can create multipath ghost targets, and water films on a radome can attenuate the signal. A sensor suite must therefore qualify the remaining radar coverage when optical observations degrade.

### Out-of-distribution inputs at the sensor boundary

A structurally valid observation from an unoccluded, calibrated sensor can still lie outside the conditions on which the models downstream were qualified. Its uncertainty has two sources. **Aleatoric uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!aleatoric} is the irreducible variation of the transduction itself, such as photon shot noise or aerosol scattering; it is the degradation this section has described, and the measurement's error model must carry it. **Epistemic uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!epistemic} is the model's ignorance of scenes it was never shown, such as an overturned pallet, a novel emergency strobe pattern, or an industrial smoke plume, and no amount of sensor quality removes it. Why a normalized confidence score says nothing about the second kind, and which methods give a score a stated meaning, belong to the learned proposer (@sec-brain-softmax-illusion). How a calibrated prediction set becomes a refusal to act on an ambiguous request belongs to grounding (@eq-intent-conformal-set). Perception's share is narrower. It must detect at the ingestion boundary that an input has left the support the evaluation tested, and say so in the record.

Input-support monitors do that by scoring the input, or the backbone's early features, against the qualification data. A free-energy score computed from the backbone's unnormalized logits [@liu2020energy], a Mahalanobis distance from class-conditional feature centroids [@lee2018simple], and the reconstruction residual of a small autoencoder trained only on nominal operation are all in use. Each needs a threshold calibrated against the intended inputs and the relevant anomalies, and each can miss an anomaly that happens to score as familiar. A score outside the accepted range can trigger refusal; a score inside it does not establish that the scene was interpreted correctly. These monitors implement the input-support monitor specified in @sec-evaluation-limits.

When an input-support monitor trips, the perception engine sets the `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` flag in the observation record's health bitmask. The permission path uses this flag to refuse high-speed autonomous motions, expand clearance safety buffers, or invoke deterministic supervisory takeovers. In multi-sensor configurations, this bitmask triggers cross-modal arbitration: if the optical camera sets `BIT_OPTICAL_SATURATED` or `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` while the FMCW radar maintains valid Doppler returns, the fusion pipeline demotes optical tokens and elevates radar range claims, provided the remaining modality can support the required clearance claim within its own validated conditions.

::: {#ws-perception-tesla-williston-omission .callout-war-story title="Silent perception omission (2016)"}
**Context**: A 2015 Tesla Model S\index{Incidents!Williston accident} traveling at about $74\text{ mph}$ with Traffic-Aware Cruise Control and Autosteer active struck a refrigerated semitrailer turning left across its path near Williston, Florida [@ntsb2017tesla].

**Mechanism**: The crossing-path collision lay outside the front-to-rear crash modes for which the 2015 warning and automatic braking systems were designed. NHTSA reported that automatic braking required agreement between camera and radar; unusual vehicle shapes could impede camera classification ([NHTSA ODI PE16-007](https://static.nhtsa.gov/odi/inv/2016/INCLA-PE16007-7876.PDF)).

**Impact**: The NTSB found no recorded indication that forward collision warning or automatic emergency braking detected an object, and no pre-impact braking occurred. The car passed under the trailer, which sheared off its roof (@fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash).

**Response**: The NTSB examined operational design domain limits and driver engagement as well as the collision-avoidance systems.

**Systems lesson**: An absent detection is not evidence that a crossing path is clear. A permission design must account for detection coverage and unsupported scenarios; a health flag cannot certify that every relevant object was perceived.
:::

::: {#fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Williston collision damage**: This NTSB presentation slide shows damage on the right side of the semitrailer and the roofless Tesla after the 2016 crash. The crossing-path geometry and absence of pre-impact braking come from the [NTSB accident report](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/HAR1702.pdf), not from the photographs alone. (Source: NTSB board-meeting presentation for report HAR-17/02; photographs courtesy of Florida Highway Patrol)." fig-alt="NTSB slide with two photographs: left, a refrigerated semitrailer with damage low on its right side; right, a heavily damaged roofless Tesla. Yellow ovals mark damage areas. The photos do not show the vehicles' motion or collision angle."}
![](images/png/fig08_real_ntsb_williston_crash.png){width="90%"}
:::

Whatever record the producer attaches to an observation can expose only the faults the producer can check. The detectable faults and the timing and calibration conditions fit in such a record; silent semantic errors, like the omission at Williston, still require separate evidence.

## The Observation Contract {#sec-perception-observation-contract}

A downstream tracker, policy backbone, or the permission path cannot reconstruct exposure timing, mounting calibration, or record integrity from a raw tensor alone. The perception producer therefore wraps each observation in an **observation contract**\index{Observation contract!definition}\index{Perception!observation contract}, the sixth record of the book's fifteen-record chain. The observation is unusable without a capture epoch, a clock identifier, a bounded conversion to the permission path's clock, and a calibration inside its validity range, whose revision the frame identifier carries. The consumer refuses a record that lacks any of them before reading the payload. The clock domain and the $\mathcal{H}_1$ age budget come from the handoff record of @sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix, which this record consumes, and perception supplies the capture-side fields that let a consumer check an observation against them.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-handoff-sensor-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SENSOR-SIDE AGE AGAINST THE H_1 HANDOFF ALLOTMENT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The handoff paragraph of @sec-perception-observation-contract.
# │
# │ Goal:    Reconcile the handoff matrix's sensor-age allotment (one frame
# │          period) with this chapter's exposure-midpoint-plus-readout age.
# │ Show:    16.7 ms frame period; 24.6 ms from the top row's exposure midpoint
# │          to the end of readout; 16.3 ms from the middle row's; the top-row
# │          convention exceeds the allotment by 7.9 ms.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera frame rate, exposure, and readout. The allotment is
# │          taken as one frame period, matching the handoff matrix value.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class HandoffSensorAge:
    """Sensor-side age of the navigation camera under two row conventions."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_frame = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    age_top = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout).to(millisecond)
    age_mid = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout / 2).to(millisecond)
    excess_top = (age_top - t_frame).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_frame.magnitude - 16.7) < 0.05, f"Unexpected frame period: {t_frame}")
    check(abs(age_top.magnitude - 24.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected top-row sensor age: {age_top}")
    check(abs(age_mid.magnitude - 16.3) < 0.05, f"Unexpected middle-row sensor age: {age_mid}")
    check(age_mid < t_frame < age_top, "Prose says only the middle-row convention fits the allotment")
    check(abs(excess_top.magnitude - 7.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected excess: {excess_top}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    age_top_str = fmt_latency(age_top, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_mid_str = fmt_latency(age_mid, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    excess_top_str = fmt_latency(excess_top, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

The contract binds a raw observation tensor or an extracted bounding envelope to the fields a consumer needs to check it (@eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple):
$$\mathcal{O} = \langle t_{\text{capture}}, \text{clock\_id}, \epsilon_{\text{sync}}, \text{frame\_id}, \mathbf{T}_{\text{payload}}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, C_{\text{inset}}, \text{mask}_{\text{health}}, \text{crc32} \rangle$$ {#eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple}
Here $t_{\text{capture}}$ is the exposure-midpoint timestamp on the capture clock $\text{clock\_id}$, $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$ bounds the conversion to the permission path's clock, $\text{frame\_id}$ keys the calibrated transform, $\mathbf{T}_{\text{payload}}$ is the tensor or envelope, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is its spatial covariance, $C_{\text{inset}}$ is the qualified clearance inset, $\text{mask}_{\text{health}}$ carries the health flags, and the checksum covers header and payload. Spatial memory (@sec-memory) consumes the contract to build its spatial belief record, and trajectory planning (@sec-planning) reads its inset, so both can compute an upper age, select a valid transform, and bound spatial error before a claim shapes a proposal. The contract does not replace a serialization format such as Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, or ROS 2 IDL, and any of them can carry it. A transport schema guarantees only the layout of the data; the contract adds physical invariants a consumer can check, namely a monotonic capture epoch, a bounded clock conversion, a transform inside its validity range, and a measured error bound. @Tbl-08-observation-record-schema lists the fields with their consumer checks and fills them for the navigation camera.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-nav-observation-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAVIGATION-CAMERA OBSERVATION RECORD, FILLED
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The filled column of @tbl-08-observation-record-schema and the
# │          clock-conversion paragraph that follows it.
# │
# │ Goal:    Fill the observation record for the mobile manipulator's
# │          navigation camera and size the consumer's upper age at dispatch.
# │ Show:    age at dispatch 51.6 ms; clock-conversion bound 0.2 ms; upper
# │          age 51.8 ms, equal to the refusal threshold (budgeted age plus
# │          bound); frame counter at 60 Hz; the bound's 0.3 mm of travel at
# │          the 1.5 m/s drive limit, carried inside delta_loc rather than
# │          charged as a budget row.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age (the latency waterfall above); eps_sync is a
# │          chapter LOAD value that the spatial-belief record of @sec-memory
# │          reuses; RM.nav_camera frame rate; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class NavObservationRecord:
    """Filled observation record for the running machine's navigation camera."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX477 navigation camera)
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (capture-to-MCU clock-conversion bound; reused by @sec-memory)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    upper_age = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)
    refuse_threshold = (AISLE.perception_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # refusal threshold: budgeted age plus the conversion bound
    dx_sync = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, eps_sync).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected age at dispatch: {t_age}")
    check(abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected clock-conversion bound: {eps_sync}")
```
