```{python}
    check(abs(upper_age.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected upper age at dispatch: {upper_age}")
    check(abs(refuse_threshold.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected refusal threshold: {refuse_threshold}")
    check(abs((refuse_threshold - upper_age).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Prose says the dispatched upper age meets the refusal threshold exactly")
    check(abs(f_frame.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected navigation-camera frame rate: {f_frame}")
    check(abs(dx_sync.magnitude - 0.3) < 0.005, f"Unexpected travel during the clock-conversion bound: {dx_sync}")
    check(dx_sync < delta_loc, "Prose says the clock-conversion travel fits inside delta_loc")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    upper_age_str = fmt_latency(upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    refuse_threshold_str = fmt_latency(refuse_threshold, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    dx_sync_str = fmt_length(dx_sync, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
```

| Record field                               | Meaning                                                           | Consumer check                                                                                     | Navigation camera                                                                                                                                                        |
|:-------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `capture_timestamp_ns`, `capture_clock_id` | Exposure midpoint in one shared, monotonic capture clock          | Convert to safety microcontroller (MCU) time with a valid bounded-skew mapping before checking age | Trigger edge plus $t_{\text{exp}}/2$ (top-row exposure midpoint) on clock `cam_nav`; dispatched `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` later (@tbl-08-latency-budget) |
| `sync_error_ns`                            | Bound on capture-to-MCU clock conversion error                    | Add to worst-case age; refuse if missing or expired                                                | `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str`, so the upper age at dispatch is `{python} NavObservationRecord.upper_age_str`                                              |
| `sequence_index`                           | Monotonic camera frame counter                                    | Detect gaps and reordering                                                                         | One count per frame at `{python} NavObservationRecord.f_frame_str`                                                                                                       |
| `sensor_frame_id`                          | Transform-tree key and calibration revision                       | Select the valid extrinsic transform                                                               | `nav_cam` with its calibration revision                                                                                                                                  |
| `tensor_payload`                           | Format, dimensions, length, and buffer                            | Validate bounds and record checksum before reading                                                 | Raw/debayered image tensor or point-cloud buffer                                                                                                                         |
| `bounding_envelope`                        | Bounding volume $[dx, dy, dz]$ or qualified clearance inset       | Bound occupied volume and inflate safety sets ($C_{\text{inset}}$)                                 | Metric corridor bounds inflated by validated quantile                                                                                                                    |
| `spatial_covariance`                       | Positive-semidefinite spatial error scale                         | Use with separately calibrated bias and tail bounds                                                | Point-wise or object-centric covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}_z$                                                                                                       |
| `calibration_metadata`                     | Intrinsics, extrinsics, coefficients, temperature, validity range | Reject calibration outside its validated region                                                    | Factory pinhole $\mathbf{K}$ and chassis extrinsic transform $\mathbf{T}_{bc}$                                                                                           |
| `provenance_digest`                        | SHA-256 of firmware and model revisions                           | Match the approved build; this is not payload integrity                                            | Signed hash of vision backbone weights and firmware                                                                                                                      |
| `payload_crc32`                            | CRC over serialized header (excluding this field) and payload     | Detect accidental record corruption; not authentication                                            | 32-bit cyclical redundancy check                                                                                                                                         |
| `health_bitmask`                           | Hardware, degradation, and perception validity flags              | Refuse claims with safety-critical faults or OOD flags                                             | Sync-loss, link, saturation, rain/fog clutter, and OOD bits; input-support bits from @sec-evaluation-limits                                                              |

: **Observation contract schema**: Compact fields needed to date and frame a claim, evaluate its uncertainty, bounding envelope, and health flags, and check the bytes and generating revision. The last column fills the fields this chapter computes for the mobile manipulator's navigation camera; its dispatch age and clock-conversion bound are illustrative. A keyed authenticator is a separate requirement if the threat model includes malicious modification. {#tbl-08-observation-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[23,23,26,28]"}

The fields in @tbl-08-observation-record-schema date each observation and its generating revision. The capture timestamp is monotonic, not nanoseconds since the UNIX epoch. A rolling-shutter claim must identify the row or region whose acquisition time it represents, and `sequence_index` detects missing frames independently of clock conversion. If the MCU has a different clock, a synchronization service supplies a versioned conversion $t_{\text{MCU}}=a t_{\text{capture}}+b$, its validity interval, and the measured error bound $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$, obtained as @sec-perception-qualifying-error describes.

The handoff matrix and this chapter count the sensor's share of age differently, and the difference is a convention the record must name. The matrix allots $\mathcal{H}_1$ one frame period, `{python} HandoffSensorAge.t_frame_str` at `{python} HandoffSensorAge.f_frame_str`, and dates the frame by its middle row. From that row's exposure midpoint to the end of readout, the navigation camera's sensor-side age is $t_{\text{exp}}/2 + t_{\text{readout}}/2 =$ `{python} HandoffSensorAge.age_mid_str`, inside the allotment. The latency waterfall instead charges the top row, $t_{\text{exp}}/2 + t_{\text{readout}} =$ `{python} HandoffSensorAge.age_top_str`, because the top row is the oldest in the frame and a rack upright can occupy any row. On that oldest-row convention the camera exceeds the $\mathcal{H}_1$ allotment by `{python} HandoffSensorAge.excess_top_str`. Both numbers are correct for their purpose: the handoff matrix tracks the typical row, while a stopping budget must charge the oldest row its claim rests on. The record's capture timestamp therefore names its row, so a consumer knows which convention it received and can add the difference when it needs the other.

At dispatch, the producer records the upper age $t_{\text{MCU,dispatch}}-t_{\text{MCU,capture}}+\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$. That value describes a past checkpoint. At admission, the evidence is older by $\Delta_{\text{da}}$; at later consumption it is older still. The permission path must use its current monotonic time and the original capture epoch, rather than replaying the dispatch-age value as if physical time had stopped. A new proposal based on the same observation does not refresh its evidence.

For the navigation camera, the **dispatch-local** threshold is `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` plus the `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str` conversion bound, or `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str`. The illustrative frame reaches that threshold exactly at dispatch, leaving no extra dispatch-stage allowance for batching or host contention. The budget charges the `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` pipeline interval as distance; the clock bound's `{python} NavObservationRecord.dx_sync_str` travel is carried inside $\delta_{\text{loc}}$. Neither convention removes post-dispatch physical aging.

Admission requires a separately qualified current-age limit that includes the dispatch-to-admission bound and leaves room for the active lease and physical response. The present partial ledger has not established that limit, so the filled record demonstrates qualified field construction, not an admitted full-speed trajectory. Once $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ is bounded, the engineer can close the stopping calculation or reduce speed to recover margin. Each elapsed interval appears once: if a budget starts at admission, it includes the prior evidence age plus the subsequent lease; if it starts at capture, it accounts for the same timeline without adding those intervals again.

The transform key and calibration revision anchor metric coordinates.[^fn-stereo-baseline-thermal] The firmware/model digest supports version provenance; `payload_crc32` detects accidental changes to the actual header and payload after serialization. Neither a checksum nor a build hash proves semantic truth, and neither authenticates an adversarial producer without a keyed check.

[^fn-stereo-baseline-thermal]: **Stereo Baseline Thermal Drift**\index{Hardware!thermal expansion}: For a stereo baseline $b =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str` and an unmodeled change $|\delta b| =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.db_str`, first-order geometry gives $|\delta z|/z\approx|\delta b|/b$. At $z =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.z_thermal_str`, the corresponding depth bias is about `{python} StereoDepthError.dz_thermal_str`, assuming focal length and disparity are otherwise unchanged. Temperature compensation must be checked against the actual mount and calibration.

In the health bitmask, the lower bits report hardware faults such as synchronization loss or transport errors; intermediate bits report environmental degradation (such as lens saturation or aerosol backscatter); and the upper bits report perceptual validity concerns such as occlusion or out-of-distribution inputs outside the support the evaluation tested. These input-support bits implement the runtime monitor specified in @sec-evaluation-limits. A set safety-critical bit requires refusal of the affected claim.

The explicit record layout also supports fault injection. A test can alter the capture time, omit a sequence number, inflate reported covariance, or set an occlusion flag, then check whether the consumer rejects or degrades that claim within its budget. Such mutations verify response to the injected record faults; physical glare, miscalibration, and actuator behavior still require separate tests in @sec-verification.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Observation contract mutations feed the hardware-in-the-loop verification harness in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

A learned consumer needs these fields as much as an estimator does. A policy $\mathbf{a}_t = \pi(\mathbf{z}_{t_0})$ that receives neither the elapsed time since capture nor the current state cannot distinguish two identical images consumed after different delays. Widely used VLAs do not supply that information: RT-2 and OpenVLA condition on images and language [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla], and $\pi_0$ adds the robot's proprioceptive state [@black2024pi0], but none encodes capture age, sensor extrinsics, or measurement covariance. This book therefore proposes an **observation tokenizer** that exposes the record itself to a VLA policy or neural state estimator. The modality determines the payload: image features, metric returns, motion events, or contact deformation. The common interface preserves when and where that payload was measured and what uncertainty accompanies it.

In the proposed interface, the observation tokenizer binds the sensory payload token $\mathbf{z}_{\text{sensor}}$ with continuous temporal positional embeddings ($\mathbf{e}_{\Delta t} = \text{Fourier}(t_{\text{current}} - t_0)$), coordinate frame prefix embeddings ($\mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}} = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{T}_{bc})$), and spatial covariance tokens ($\mathbf{e}_{\Sigma} = \text{MLP}(\text{vec}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_z))$) (@eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer):
$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{token}} = [\mathbf{z}_{\text{sensor}}, \mathbf{e}_{\Delta t}, \mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}}, \mathbf{e}_{\Sigma}]$$ {#eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer}
A forward-propagated state token, $\mathbf{e}_{\text{state}} = \text{MLP}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{\text{current}}})$ from the estimator of @sec-perception-state-estimation, can join them so the policy conditions on where the machine is at execution rather than at capture. This representation makes time, frame, and uncertainty available to the learned model; it does not show that the model uses them. The evidence would be an ablation that injects known delays into held-out episodes and compares closed-loop error with and without the timing tokens. Qualification still depends on the clock, calibration, residual, and health checks; encoding their values as tokens cannot replace those checks.

::: {#chk-percep-observation-contract-triage .callout-checkpoint title="Observation record checks"}

A consumer can refuse only what the record lets it check, and it must check before it reads the payload.

- [ ] **Record triage**: Can you explain why a health bit, checksum, valid clock conversion, and freshness check must precede consumption of a spatial claim?
- [ ] **Timestamp corruption vs. dropped packets**: Can you describe why receiving a sensory frame with a desynchronized timestamp degrades spatial state estimation and policy grounding far more severely than dropping the packet entirely?
- [ ] **Deterministic fault injection**: Can you distinguish between physically perturbing optical sensors vs. deterministically mutating fields in the shared-memory observation record during automated hardware-in-the-loop verification?
- [ ] **Batch-age estimate**: If the navigation camera's frames were batched in pairs at its `{python} TemporalBatching.f_frame_str` cadence, what would the older frame's dispatch age be, and would it meet the `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str` dispatch-local threshold?

:::

Because the record keeps the capture epoch, even an observation that arrives late remains usable: an estimator can apply it at the instant it describes and replay the correction to the present, which @sec-perception-discrete-state-estimation develops. Neither that update nor a passed record check proves that the observation is semantically correct; the following mistakes confuse qualified representation with physical truth.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-perception-fallacies-pitfalls}

Perception\index{Perception} must describe the world within the strict temporal deadlines required for control actuation. Semantic confidence and high spatial accuracy cannot compensate for pipelines that deliver stale observations, fuse asynchronous exposures, or read average bandwidth as a bound on one frame's age.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Accepting an observation because its semantic classification confidence is high, regardless of its age.*

The mobile manipulator receives a high-confidence observation that the rack end ahead is clear, but a stall in the vision pipeline\index{Perception!pipeline latency} delivers it several frames late. A person who stepped out after the exposure is absent from that frame. The confidence score\index{Confidence score} describes the earlier image, not present clearance. Accepting the packet as current can therefore authorize motion toward an occupied rack end. The perception interface must check measurement age against its refusal threshold (@sec-perception-observation-contract)\index{Observation!freshness limit} and reject observations that exceed it. Any continued state propagation\index{State estimation!propagation} without new data must carry kinematic uncertainty covariances\index{Kinematics!uncertainty} together with qualified residual tails or hard bounds on dynamic-obstacle reachability, allowing the controller to enforce safety envelopes\index{Safety!envelope} as historical evidence ages. *A softmax score certifies neither distribution membership, temporal freshness, nor physical clearance.*

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Fusing multi-sensor observations without a clock bound derived from the tolerated spatial error.*

Two cameras on the mobile manipulator watch the same rack upright while the base drives at its `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` drive limit, but their clocks differ by $\Delta t_{\text{skew}}$. Treating the two exposure times\index{Exposure time} as equal places the upright $v\,\Delta t_{\text{skew}}$ apart in the two views, and track association\index{Track association} can then split one physical object into two conflicting tracks ("ghosting"). Spatial calibration\index{Calibration!spatial} cannot correct an unknown temporal offset. The synchronization requirement must follow the tolerated position error and maximum relevant speed, expressed by $\Delta t_{\text{skew}} \le \epsilon_{\text{pos}} / v_{\text{max}}$. Hardware synchronization\index{Hardware!clock synchronization} at exposure time makes that bound enforceable; selecting a timing technology (like Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588 PTP\index{IEEE 1588 PTP}) without first checking the spatial error budget leaves the fusion assumption unverified.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Inferring a critical read's deadline from average camera bandwidth.*

An acceptable average utilization says nothing about how long one read waits behind a synchronized capture and inference burst. On the mobile manipulator no permission-path read waits behind the burst, because the microcontroller reads from its own memory; the burst instead ages the frame or delays the chunk that the application processor is preparing (@sec-perception-cost-ingestion), so the quantities to verify under the synchronized burst are the host's capture-to-dispatch age and its renewal interval, not its average bandwidth.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming an end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy implicitly learns to compensate for rolling shutter and sensor latency without explicit temporal tokenization.*

A common assumption in deep imitation learning is that large vision-language-action policies trained on extensive robot teleoperation datasets will automatically learn to predict actions that compensate for image distortion and communication latency. In practice, demonstration datasets are collected under varying chassis velocities, camera modes, and host bus loads. Because the model receives only raw pixels without capture timestamps or row readout indices, the network cannot disambiguate physical obstacle geometry from rolling-shutter scanline shearing or latency-induced travel. Such ambiguity can compound closed-loop errors. The familiar $O(T^2 \epsilon)$ behavior-cloning bound concerns accumulated cost under its assumptions, with horizon $T$ and imitation error $\epsilon$; it is not a universal spatial-error or oscillation law. Capture time deltas ($\Delta t = t_{\text{current}} - t_0$) and propagated kinematic state can expose the missing information. Explicit tokenization is one implementation; evaluation must establish its effectiveness, and independent permission checks remain necessary.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating neural depth network outputs as calibrated geometric covariances without empirical residual validation.*

Monocular depth estimation backbones and BEV lifting transformers output continuous depth maps or discrete depth-bin categorical distributions. Engineers often mistake these softmax distributions or network confidence heads for calibrated geometric uncertainties ($\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$), passing them directly to Kalman filters (@sec-perception-state-estimation) or safety barrier functions (@sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission). However, neural depth scores are uncalibrated model confidences that correlate poorly with true physical error tails. On novel textures, specular reflections, or edge silhouettes, depth networks produce gross multimodal outliers that lie dozens of standard deviations from ground truth. Downstream clearance insets ($C_{\text{inset}}$) must never rely on raw neural variance; they require empirical validation against heavy-tailed residual distributions and hard bounds verified by active ranging sensors (LiDAR or radar).

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying exclusively on line-of-sight optical sensing for manipulation without tactile contact feedback.*

During some reaches and grasps, the robot's end-effector structures (fingers, palm, and wrist) occlude the contact region. Optical cameras cannot observe contact normal forces, shear stress distributions, or incipient micro-slip at the physical boundary. Assuming that high-resolution visual perception alone can guarantee grasp stability leads to dropped fragile objects or excessive motor torques that crush delicate structures. A task that depends on detecting slip or contact forces at that occluded patch needs suitable contact evidence. Tactile sensing such as elastomeric shear tracking can supply it; other tasks may instead rely on qualified force sensing, constrained fixtures, or passive grasp mechanics. The required feedback follows the contact decision, not a universal sensor prescription.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming active LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to specular reflections and multipath interference in built environments.*

Engineers frequently assume that because LiDAR and active depth sensors emit their own structured energy, they are impervious to optical lighting pitfalls. In physical industrial settings with polished concrete floors, metallic shelving, architectural glass, and shrink-wrapped freight, active beams violate the diffuse Lambertian scattering assumption. Emitted pulses undergo specular forward reflection, producing artificial zero-return dropouts ("puddle black holes") on wet or polished floors, while multi-bounce reflections generate phantom obstacles located meters behind walls or beneath the floor plane. The observation pipeline must validate return intensity distributions and cross-corroborate surface geometry against inertial and radar channels.

:::

## Summary {#sec-perception-summary}

A perception result is usable only when its capture time, clock conversion, coordinate frame, and error qualification fit the proposed motion. Sensor choice starts from the physical quantity the decision needs. Capture physics then fixes the instant and geometry a measurement describes, from the exposure midpoint and the row-by-row timing of a rolling shutter to the bearing ray that carries no range until stereo or active ranging supplies it, and every calibration holds only inside the conditions it was fitted under. The navigation camera's capture-to-dispatch age contributes a concrete stopping-budget term, but evidence keeps aging through proposal computation, transport, and admission, an interval the filled dispatch record does not close until a measured dispatch-to-admission bound joins the ledger. Dating a frame by arrival or freezing its age at dispatch hides elapsed time; neither restores physical clearance.

Spatial error is spent from the same clearance. Stereo depth error grows with squared range under fixed disparity noise, and an extrinsic shift adds a lever-arm error that grows with distance. The error a claim reports is itself a claim to be measured. A residual quantile measured against ground truth sets the clearance inset and includes the bias a covariance omits, and the clock bound comes from measurement rather than a datasheet. Neither a covariance nor a learned depth score supplies a 99th-percentile clearance bound by itself. Perception's output ends there, at a single dated, framed, and qualified measurement; fusing such measurements into a state that stays current between them is the work of the estimator that spatial memory runs.

The failures that matter most are the silent ones, from a misdated frame to a saturated image or a hallucinated clear path, because none of them raises a fault flag. The observation contract lets the consumer refuse whatever it can check before reading the payload (capture epoch, clock conversion, frame, calibration, integrity, and health), and semantic truth still requires independent evidence.

Seven relations carry the chapter's quantitative argument, and @tbl-08-key-equations records what each bounds or decides.

| Equation                                                                                           | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                              | Derived                          |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| $\Delta \mathbf{x} = \int_{t_0}^{t_0+t_{\text{age}}} \mathbf{v}(t)\,dt$                            | The travel an observation's age costs before any consumer can react; at constant speed, $v\,t_{\text{age}}$ enters the stopping budget | @eq-percep-spatial-displacement  |
| $t_{\text{age}} = \tfrac{1}{2}t_{\text{exp}} + t_{\text{readout}} + \dots + t_{\text{IPC}}$        | The capture-to-dispatch age of serialized stages, and which stage dominates it; overlapping stages need a measured interval instead    | @eq-percep-latency-waterfall     |
| $\Delta x(y) = v\,y\,t_{\text{row}}$                                                               | The along-track shear a rolling shutter records, which must be removed before the estimator spends $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ on it         | @eq-percep-rolling-shutter-skew  |
| $\lvert\delta z\rvert \approx \dfrac{z^2}{f b}\lvert\delta d\rvert$                                | How fast stereo depth error grows with range, and so the range beyond which one standard deviation consumes an allowance               | @eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty    |
| $C_{\text{inset}} = C_{\text{safe}} + \lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}\rVert_{P_{99}}$ | The clearance a consumer holds so the true obstacle stays outside $C_{\text{safe}}$ except with the measured tail probability          | @eq-percep-clearance-inset       |
| $\Delta p = v\,\delta t + \tfrac{1}{2} a\,(\delta t)^2$                                            | The position error a misdated observation carries silently, the reason a wrong timestamp is worse than a lost frame                    | @eq-percep-kinematic-drift       |
| $k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$                                                                | Which sorted residual sets a clearance inset with coverage $1-\alpha$, and the fewest residuals that can set one                       | @sec-perception-qualifying-error |

: **Key equations of sensor perception**: The relations that turn a sensor's timing and geometry into travel and spatial error, and set the clearance a consumer holds, with the place each is derived. {#tbl-08-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[36,46,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Spatial perception and age of information"}
* **Observation Age Begins at Capture and Is Paid in Travel:**\index{Perception!observation age}\index{Perception!blind distance} Hardware-latched exposure time, row timing when relevant, and bounded clock conversion let the consumer compute an upper age. Every interval from capture to actuator response becomes unobserved travel ($d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}}$) spent from the same clearance.
* **Choose the Measurement for the Decision:**\index{Perception!multimodal fusion} Appearance, metric range, radial velocity, changing edges, and contact deformation answer different physical questions. Complementary sensors help only when their coverage and correlated failure modes have been qualified.
* **Fix the Geometry Before Interpreting It:**\index{Hardware!rolling shutter}\index{Perception!calibration drift} Rolling-shutter readout shears straight edges under motion ($\Delta x = v \cdot y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$) and must be removed with per-row poses before triangulation. Calibration can change too. The chapter's `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_ext_str` rad extrinsic shift at `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.z_ext_str` projects to `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dx_ext_str` laterally, as large as the whole $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ allowance, so every calibration carries a validity range the consumer checks.
* **A Wrong Timestamp Is Worse Than a Lost Frame:**\index{Perception!timestamp integrity} A dropped frame is visibly missing; a plausible but misdated frame places the obstacle where it never stood while claiming the same spread. Hardware capture stamps, clock bounds, sequence counters, and age checks must precede any use of the payload.
* **Claimed Error Must Be Measured:**\index{Machine Learning!geometric uncertainty} A classification or depth-bin score is not a spatial tail, and a covariance is not a clearance bound. Residuals measured against ground truth set the inset, and those residuals include the bias a covariance omits.
* **The Record Bounds What a Consumer Can Refuse:**\index{Perception!observation contract}\index{Perception!silent failure}\index{Perception!dated snapshots} The observation contract carries epoch, clock bound, frame, calibration, error, and health so the permission path can refuse a claim before reading its payload. A healthy sensor can still describe a clear path that is not there, and typed observation tokens do not prove that a learned policy compensates for delay. Semantic truth needs independent evidence, and spatial memory must fuse each dated snapshot into a state and carry it through occlusion.
:::

Perception makes useful action possible by locating obstacles, identifying candidate contacts, and measuring range and motion with complementary sensors. Its output is evidence tied to a capture time and geometric frame, one measurement at a time. Once a person passes behind the rack, the machine must turn those measurements into a state, preserve what they support, and account for what could have changed out of view.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-perception-history}

The camera geometry of this chapter came to machine vision from photogrammetry, which calibrated cameras for mapping long before robots carried them. @tsai1987versatile made accurate calibration possible with off-the-shelf television cameras and lenses, and @zhang2000flexible reduced it to showing the camera a printed planar pattern in a few orientations, which turned calibration from a laboratory procedure into a routine step. @hartley2003multiple gathered the multiple-view geometry on which stereo depth and its error rest. Hand-eye calibration [@shiu1989calibration; @tsai1989new] extended the problem to cameras that move with an arm, and @furgale2013unified added time to the unknowns, estimating the camera-to-IMU offset together with the rotation and translation. Each step moved toward the position this chapter takes: a calibration is an estimate with its own error and validity range, not a constant read from a drawing.

The sensors diversified along the same line. The autonomous-driving competitions of the mid-2000s made scanning laser range the default metric sensor for mobile robots [@thrun2006stanley], and the spinning multi-beam LiDAR brought with it the sweep distortion and per-point stamps of @sec-perception-lidar-age. Neuromorphic engineering [@mead1990] produced a pixel that reports change instead of level [@lichtsteiner2008128], and a decade of work on estimation and learning with such sensors [@gallego2022event] showed both their timing advantage and their blindness to a static scene. Time itself became a measured quantity. Agreement among clocks was a distributed-systems problem before it was a sensing one [@lamport1978time], and the Precision Time Protocol [@ieee15882002; @ieee15882019] made hardware time stamping at the network interface the basis of clock agreement among networked sensors, which is what lets the machine's LiDAR stamp every column on a clock the permission path can convert.

The last ingredient is the qualification of error. Conformal prediction [@vovk2005algorithmic] showed that exchangeable calibration residuals give a distribution-free bound with a stated coverage, and @angelopoulos2023gentle made the split-conformal rule used for the clearance inset a routine tool. The observation record joins these lineages: it carries the calibration revision, the clock bound, and the measured tail so that a consumer can check each of them instead of trusting the sensor that produced them.

For further reading, six works cover the chapter's geometry, timing, and error qualification.

- @hartley2003multiple is the standard reference for projection, epipolar geometry, and triangulation, and the source of the stereo error relations in @sec-perception-error-clearance.
- @szeliski2022computer surveys image formation, calibration, and stereo from the image-processing side, including the lens and sensor effects behind @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
- @zhang2000flexible is short and shows how a planar target recovers intrinsics and distortion, the procedure behind every calibration revision the observation record carries.
- @furgale2013unified estimates spatial and temporal calibration jointly and shows why a camera-to-IMU time offset must be treated as an unknown rather than assumed zero.
- @gallego2022event reviews event sensing from pixel circuit to algorithms, with the timing and static-scene trade-offs that decide whether an event camera fits a clearance claim.
- @angelopoulos2023gentle introduces conformal prediction with the exchangeability assumption stated plainly, the assumption a floor refinish or lighting change breaks.

## Problems {#sec-perception-problems}

```{python}
#| label: perception-problems
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ END-OF-CHAPTER PROBLEM GIVENS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-perception-problems.
# │ Goal:    Print each problem's givens from the registry and the chapter's
# │          cells, and guard the property each problem depends on, so a
# │          registry change cannot silently turn an intended answer around.
# │ Show:    givens only (answers live in the private instructor solutions):
# │          one-tenth allowance share; batches of 2 to 4; 4 m stereo range;
# │          500 residuals; 10 Hz LiDAR mode; Unitree H1 top speed 3.3 m/s.
# │ How:     Reuses SensorInformationAge, RollingShutterSkew, StereoDepthError,
# │          ExtrinsicErrorBudget, ErrorQualification, LidarAge,
# │          NavObservationRecord, and TemporalBatching; recomputes each
# │          guarded property.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_frequency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
H1 = Embodied.Humanoid.Unitree_H1

class PerceptionProblems:
    """Givens for the Chapter 8 problems, with guards on the answers they imply."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    share = 0.10  # category: illustrative (problem given: share of an allowance one error may spend)
    shadow_acc = 0.97  # category: illustrative (problem given: a claimed shadow accuracy)
    z_stereo = 4.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (problem given: stereo claim range)
    n_resid = 500  # category: illustrative (problem given: residuals collected)
    alpha_strict = 0.001  # category: illustrative (problem given: a stricter tail)
    f_lidar_slow = RM.lidar.scan_rate / 2  # category: datasheet (the OS1's 10 Hz mode)
    v_h1 = H1.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: datasheet (registry: Unitree H1 top speed)
    width = RM.footprint_width  # category: illustrative (base footprint width)
    wrist = RM.wrist_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX296, global shutter)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)
    t_frame = (1 / RM.nav_camera.frame_rate).to(millisecond)
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)
    thr = NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold
    age_2 = (t_age + t_frame).to(millisecond)  # P1: batches of 2, 3, 4
    age_3 = (t_age + 2 * t_frame).to(millisecond)
    age_4 = (t_age + 3 * t_frame).to(millisecond)
    cut_needed = (age_2 - thr).to(millisecond)  # P1: backbone cut for a pair to pass
    budget = (share * AISLE.delta_loc).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_readout_max = (budget / v).to(millisecond)  # P2
    v_max_rs = (budget / RM.nav_camera.readout_time).to(meter / second)  # P2
    theta_max = (budget / AISLE.d_clear).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude  # P3, rad
    b_needed = (z_stereo**2 * StereoDepthError.sigma_d_px / (StereoDepthError.f_px * budget)).to(meter)  # P4
    n_min_strict = math.ceil((1 - alpha_strict) / alpha_strict)  # P5
    k_500 = math.ceil((n_resid + 1) * (1 - ErrorQualification.alpha))
    t_sync_max = (share * NavObservationRecord.eps_sync / (ErrorQualification.drift_ppm * 1e-6)).to(second)  # P5
    t_sweep_slow = (1 / f_lidar_slow).to(millisecond)  # P6
    age_stream_slow = (t_sweep_slow * LidarAge.sector_deg / 360 + LidarAge.t_data + LidarAge.eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    age_full_slow = (t_sweep_slow + LidarAge.t_data + LidarAge.eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    dx_h1 = (v_h1 * t_age).to(ureg.millimeter)  # P7
    skew_h1 = (v_h1 * RM.nav_camera.readout_time).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_age_h1 = (SensorInformationAge.row_age / v_h1).to(millisecond)
    sensor_side = (RM.nav_camera.exposure_time / 2 + RM.nav_camera.readout_time).to(millisecond)
    wrist_side = (wrist.exposure_time / 2 + wrist.readout_time).to(millisecond)  # P8

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(min(age_2, age_3, age_4) > thr, "P1: every batch of two or more must fail the dispatch-local threshold.")
    check(cut_needed < AISLE.t_backbone, "P1: the pair must be rescuable only by cutting most of the backbone stage.")
    check(t_readout_max < RM.nav_camera.readout_time / 4, "P2: the navigation camera must miss the readout target by more than 4x.")
    check(
        theta_max < math.radians(0.5) and theta_max < LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep.to(radian).magnitude,
        "P3: the tolerable mount error must be far below one LiDAR sweep's yaw.",
    )
    check(b_needed > width, "P4: the required baseline must exceed the base's width.")
    check(n_min_strict == 999 and k_500 == 496, f"P5: conformal answers drifted: {n_min_strict}, {k_500}.")
    check(abs(t_sync_max.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"P5: sync interval drifted: {t_sync_max}.")
    check(age_full_slow > t_age and age_stream_slow < t_age, "P6: in the 10 Hz mode only streaming must stay younger than the camera.")
    check(
        skew_h1 > AISLE.delta_loc and t_age_h1 < sensor_side,
        "P7: the humanoid must overrun delta_loc and need an age below the camera's sensor-side age.",
    )
    check(wrist.shutter_type == "global" and wrist_side < sensor_side, "P8: the wrist camera must be global shutter with a shorter sensor-side age.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    share_pct_str = fmt_percent(share, precision=0)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    z_stereo_str = fmt_length(z_stereo, unit=meter, precision=0)
    n_resid_str = fmt_int(n_resid)
    alpha_strict_pct_str = fmt(alpha_strict * 100, precision=1)
    f_lidar_slow_str = fmt_frequency(f_lidar_slow, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    v_h1_str = fmt_velocity(v_h1, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    width_str = fmt_length(width.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=0)
    wrist_exp_str = fmt_latency(wrist.exposure_time.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wrist_readout_str = fmt_latency(wrist.readout_time.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wrist_rate_str = fmt_frequency(wrist.frame_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    sweep_yaw_str = LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep_str
    shadow_acc_pct_str = fmt_percent(shadow_acc, precision=0)
```

Each problem states its givens, which come from the machine card (@tbl-01-machine-card), from this chapter's calculations, or from the MLSysIM registry. A given marked illustrative is an assumption for the exercise, not a measurement. The tag names the kind of work, and the parenthesis names the learning objective the problem assesses.

1. **[Compute]** (Capture-to-dispatch age) The navigation camera runs at `{python} TemporalBatching.f_frame_str` and dispatches a single frame `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` after its exposure midpoint (@tbl-08-latency-budget). A team batches consecutive frames in groups of two, three, and four (illustrative) to raise accelerator throughput. Compute the dispatch age of each batch's oldest frame and decide which batches meet the `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str` dispatch-local threshold. How much must the `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str` backbone stage shrink before a batch of two passes, and what does that imply for batching the rack-end claim?
2. **[Compute]** (Rolling shutter) Suppose one uncorrected error may spend at most `{python} PerceptionProblems.share_pct_str` percent of $\delta_{\text{loc}} =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` (illustrative), or `{python} PerceptionProblems.budget_str`. Using @eq-percep-rolling-shutter-skew, find the longest readout that keeps the along-track skew within that share at the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit, and compare it with the navigation camera's `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_readout_str`. At the camera's actual readout, what speed would meet the same share? Decide whether the machine should buy a faster sensor, drive slower, or correct the skew, and state what the correction requires.
3. **[Compute]** (Calibration) With the same `{python} PerceptionProblems.budget_str` share, find the largest mounting-angle error that keeps the lever-arm error of a point at the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.z_upright_str` rack-end range within it, in milliradians and degrees. Compare it with the `{python} PerceptionProblems.sweep_yaw_str` mrad the base yaws during one LiDAR sweep in @sec-perception-transduction-calibration, and explain why de-skew must precede any check of the LiDAR's extrinsic calibration.
4. **[Compute]** (Clearance evaluation) Keep the stereo rig of \ref{nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall}. What baseline would hold one standard deviation of depth error at `{python} PerceptionProblems.z_stereo_str` to the `{python} PerceptionProblems.budget_str` share? Compare it with the base's `{python} PerceptionProblems.width_str` footprint width, and with the OS1-64's `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_min_str` to `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_max_str` range precision. Decide which sensor should carry a clearance claim at that range, and what must still be measured before either one sets $C_{\text{inset}}$.
5. **[Compute]** (Qualifying error) Using the split-conformal rule of @sec-perception-qualifying-error, find the fewest residuals that can set a bound at a `{python} PerceptionProblems.alpha_strict_pct_str` percent tail (illustrative), and which sorted residual sets the `{python} ErrorQualification.alpha_pct_str` percent bound from `{python} PerceptionProblems.n_resid_str` residuals (illustrative). Then find the longest sync interval that keeps the OS1-64's `{python} ErrorQualification.drift_ppm_str` ppm drift within `{python} PerceptionProblems.share_pct_str` percent of the `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str` clock-conversion bound. State which of these numbers the datasheet can supply and which only a measurement campaign can.
6. **[Compute]** (Capture-to-dispatch age, LiDAR) The OS1-64 can also run at `{python} PerceptionProblems.f_lidar_slow_str` (illustrative choice of mode). Repeat @tbl-08-lidar-age for that mode: the forward-sector time, and the upper age before processing when streaming the sector and when waiting for the full sweep. How much processing time does each policy leave before the LiDAR claim is older than the camera's `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`? Decide whether the slower mode is acceptable for the rack-end check.
7. **[Compute]** (Transfer to a humanoid) A Unitree H1 humanoid, whose registry top speed is `{python} PerceptionProblems.v_h1_str`, carries the same navigation camera and pipeline. Compute the travel during the `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` dispatch age and the along-track rolling-shutter skew at that speed. What dispatch age would hold the travel to the warehouse machine's `{python} SensorInformationAge.row_age_str`, and can this camera reach it given that exposure midpoint and readout alone take `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_readout_str`? Name the assumption of the warehouse machine that the humanoid breaks and the design change it forces.
8. **[Design]** (Observation record) Fill @tbl-08-observation-record-schema for the machine's wrist camera, a global-shutter sensor running at `{python} PerceptionProblems.wrist_rate_str` with a `{python} PerceptionProblems.wrist_exp_str` exposure and `{python} PerceptionProblems.wrist_readout_str` readout (registry). Give its sensor-side age from the exposure midpoint to the end of readout and state which row convention the record names. Mark every field whose value this chapter does not supply and name the measurement that would supply it.
9. **[Design]** (Modality selection) The machine will also work a loading-dock aisle where afternoon sun enters through open doors and the floor is often wet. For the rack-end claim, which needs metric range to an occupied region inside the `{python} LidarAge.d_clear_str` clear distance, choose a primary and a corroborating modality from @tbl-08-sensor-modalities. For each candidate you reject, name the failure mode from @sec-perception-failure-modes that rules it out, and specify the health-bitmask flags the record must carry for the modalities you keep.
10. **[Critique]** (Learned depth) A team feeds a monocular depth network's per-pixel predicted spread into the observation record as $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and sets $C_{\text{inset}}$ from it, reporting a `{python} StereoDepthError.c_ray_str` ray clearance plus two predicted standard deviations. Identify what the design omits, specify the residual campaign that would qualify an inset (ground truth, conditions, sample size from the conformal rule, and what breaks exchangeability), and state what the permission path must do until that campaign exists.
11. **[Critique]** (Metric vs. semantic evidence) A slow semantic scene model labels a LiDAR return inside the stopping envelope as a shadow, and the planner deletes the return from its occupancy input. The team argues that the model is `{python} PerceptionProblems.shadow_acc_pct_str` percent accurate on shadows in its test set (illustrative). Using the metric veto invariant (\ref{psp-perception-metric-veto-invariant}), write the review comment, and specify the test that would settle whether the deletion may ever be allowed.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From sensory photons to spatial memory"}
Perception delivers dated, qualified measurements, but the person at the rack end does not stay in view between them. @Sec-memory fuses those measurements into an estimated state, carries the estimate and its uncertainty across the gaps, and sets the expiry that lets the permission path refuse a claim once occlusion or age has exhausted the validated motion margin.
:::
